body.text: The recent passing away of the Barbadian cricketing giant Garfield Sobers, days short of his 90th birthday, signifies not just a huge sporting loss but the disappearance of a Black icon whose urgency lay in the influence he exerted beyond the playing field. That a game invented by the British for leisure at home and used to impose psychological overlordship on their overseas colonies should have thrown up in Sobers—or before him in Learie Constantine or George Headley—immaculate expressions of skill, perseverance, and athleticism, no doubt had a dampening effect on white arrogance. At the same time, the towering presence of someone like Sobers brought joy and pride to not just the peoples of the Caribbean but Black and brown men and women across the cricketing world. It is not for nothing that whenever we talk of Black Pride, we never fail to doff our caps, hats, turbans, or whatever, to the superlative likes of Sobers, Frank Worrell, Muhammad Ali, Arthur Ashe, Wilma Rudolph, Althea Gibson, or Jesse Owens. In a real sense, in honouring them, we honour the tyrannised and subjugated man’s spirited resolve not to give in, however formidable the odds.

I was a lad of 10 when the West Indies played a comparatively unimportant match at the Keenan Stadium in my hometown of Jamshedpur. The visitors were a long line of brilliant Black cricketers, from Conrad Hunte and Rohan Kanhai to Sobers and Collie Smith, but perhaps due to a racist bias, the team was led by a white wicketkeeper named Franz Alexander, popularly known as Gerry. Sobers, already a star, was rested for the Test match to be played at the Eden Gardens in Calcutta, days after the Jamshedpur match. But Kanhai and Smith, and others of the calibre of Basil Butcher, Joe Solomon, or Lance Gibbs, were seen in action, hitting the ball or spinning the cherry as they wished. I remember that the popular discontent over not being able to see Sobers in action was the most significant feature of the match won by the visitors without shedding a drop of sweat.
A filmmaker from Trinidad

Almost half a century later, I came across a smiling, happy-go-lucky London-based Trinidadian filmmaker of Indian origin at a rooftop party in Hotel Horizon, across the road from the state-owned Kairali Theatre. Horace Ové is no more, having passed away in London some years after our meeting, but memories remain of a director who held his drink with humour and grace but also wore his reputation lightly. Ové’s film Playing Away (35 mm, colour, 100 minutes, 1986) uses a cricket match in the English countryside between an all-white team and a visiting side composed mostly of Black men to punch holes gently and well into racial and other stereotypes. The film looks surprisingly modern, perhaps because so little seems to have changed in the way Black and white people in Britain, or anywhere else for that matter, still view each other. A film laden with humour at each other’s expense, a little anger and some suspicion, and jabs at varied idiosyncrasies of either community, Playing Away looks conventional on the surface, but can be complex and, therefore, that much more engaging if one is prepared/equipped to read between the layers and the lines.

Ové was of part Indian origin: his grandmother was Hindu and grandfather Muslim, both made to work as indentured labourers. Added to this were other genetic contributions, including Black and Spanish. Ové’s words spring at me from my well-preserved scrapbook: “My mixed lineage has given me the confidence to fight against any form of racism.” One of the foremost Black independent filmmakers in Britain, Ové’s first films date back to the 1960s, when race relations were far more problem-ridden than they are today. Saluting the director, the British Film Institute had said: “Horace Ove is undoubtedly a pioneer in Black British history and his work provides a perspective on the Black experience in Britain.”

By his own admission, Ové learnt what serious good movies are by repeatedly watching Federico Fellini, Michelangelo Antonioni, Satyajit Ray, and other masters. On his third or fourth drink at the Horizon, he wondered aloud why “no one has anything to say about Ray at Indian film festivals these days”. He continued: “Ray did not make popular movies, but he made some great movies which have given people like me hours and hours of pleasurable viewing.”

Ové had other connections with India. It was not until the mid-1980s that he came to India for the first time to make what turned out to be two widely appreciated works. His documentation of the Bhopal gas tragedy with its national and international implications was the first of these. The other related to the fantastic, almost mythical lives of the tiffin-carriers of Bombay who would arrange to feed lakhs of office-goers each working day, helped by mental calculations that, according to Ové, would put the most developed computers to shame. Ové also directed, for a BBC series, an episode on the struggles and sacrifice of the great revolutionary Udham Singh.
Ancestral homelands

Ové was born in Trinidad but lived the greater part of his life in London. It is possible that the stories he heard as a child from his migrant Indian grandparents persuaded him to return to the land of his ancestors more than once to do films of social and historical value. But the same cannot be said of Michelle Mohabeer, the Guyana-born, Toronto-based filmmaker, at least two of whose early works have been screened in India. Her ancestors, too, had migrated from India, and although her films carry memories of exile, she has not been able to visit the land of her roots. In addition to making films, Mohabeer has been actively involved in anti-racist education work in Toronto. Her priorities and her concerns find artistic expression in her work, which, in one sense, may be said to be about lost souls on islands that are frequently and falsely described as being so many paradises on earth. Serving aboriginal people and people of colour through art is an article of faith for her.

Mohabeer has been known to quote from Edward Said in relation to the experiences of people like her, faced with the perennial trial of deciding where they belong. One such quote is: “Exile is strangely compelling to think about but terrible to experience. It is the unhealable rift forced between a human being and a native place, between the self and its true home: its essential sadness can never be surmounted.”

Coconut/Cane & Cutlass (1994, 30 minutes, b/w and colour, 16 mm) is Mohabeer’s best-known work to date. An experimental narrative, Coconut/Cane & Cutlass is an ambitious work that inspiringly articulates the Indo-Caribbean diasporic identity. Shot partially on location in Guyana and partly in a studio in Toronto, the film is a lyrical exploration of displacement, exile, and indentureship, which, replacing slavery, was in force in Guyana and in parts of the Caribbean from 1838 to 1917. This hybrid work fusing dance, poetry, theatrically staged dramatic scenes, and front-screen projected images shot on varied Guyana locations is from the point of view of an exile, an Indo-Caribbean lesbian who has been living in Canada for more than three decades. Mohabeer: “On some levels the film is partly autobiographical and partly historical… On a personal note, I am of mixed Indo-Caribbean ancestry born in Guyana… I have no idea of what part of India my ancestors were originally from.” (Excerpts from a postal interview with the director.)

According to Mohabeer, the connections forged between Indians from the Caribbean islands and India can be an important means for them to understand each other regarding their similarities and their differences. It is her hope that when Indian viewers watch her film they might be able to understand “the deep sadness and loss that is imprinted on the psyche of those of us who are displaced and exiled as a result of race, culture, sexuality and nationhood.”

Kwoi’s challenging cinematography and the reputed Lee Pui Ming’s mesmerising soundtrack (with Ravi Naimpally on the tabla) combine with ease to enhance Mohabeer’s rich, poetic style. Choreographer Florette Fernando’s energetic dance number, showing a woman at work in the cane field, is a visual delight, besides being symbolic of collective history, and is an important piece of ethnographic documentation.

Understandably, the history of struggle, sacrifice, and solidarity of the “Coolie Woman”, as those of indentured stock were called in Guyana, where she was treated worse than in other parts of the Caribbean, is at the very core of the film. By means of interview, commentary, and live footage, the point is effectively established that it was she who held home and family together. These strong, hard-working, and hard-willed people worked as domestics and gardeners; worked in rice fields and cane fields and coconut plantations, sometimes with water up to their waist; briefly, they worked wherever work was available. And, returning to their homes at night, they would tend to their vegetable gardens. The trade union movement brought some of them together, but it was ultimately the spirit of the visionary that saw them through their worst days. Mohabeer more than succeeds in bringing home to the viewer the exiled woman’s back-to-the-wall fight not to surrender any of her identities to the constant barrage of colonial hostility and attempts to humiliate her. It is no miracle that the “Coolie Woman’s” descendants now sit at many a high table of national and international importance. It is her fierce insistence on freedom from injustice that explains the transformation.
Guyana in 1953

A generation before Mohabeer made her appearance as a filmmaker, a fellow Guyanese of Indian descent by the name of Rupert Roopnaraine had directed a 75-minute documentary dating back to 1978, called The Terror and the Time. The “Terror” in the title of the film refers to British colonialism and Cold War imperialism, while the “Time” is 1953, the year the first election was held in Guyana under a provisional democratic constitution, complete with all the lacunae that come with such an exercise, and the year the British eventually suspended Guyana’s constitution. Roopnaraine’s film (35 mm, black and white and colour, 75 minutes, 1978) relates the story of the Guyanese people’s fight for independence and self-determination with readings from the poetry of Martin Carter; newspaper headlines about the Indian-origin socialist leader Cheddi Jagan and his associates struggling to defeat British conspiracies to divide the two major components of the local population—the Indians and those of African origin; newsreel footage of other struggles in the same period; and scenes of economic and cultural repression in Guyana of the 1970s. The utter destitution in which the working class, in particular, was compelled to live and work is effectively shown by Roopnaraine in agitprop style.

Roopnaraine, a political activist of no mean order, makes his resolve for change come across in every frame of this compelling documentary, which may be said to hold lessons for many countries beyond the Caribbean even today. The philosophy and aesthetics of “Third Cinema”, which produced several Latin American classics underlining the need for radical change, inform The Terror and the Time from beginning to end.

The lives and destinies of those shiploads of men and women whom the British took from Bihar and the eastern part of what we call Uttar Pradesh today—the girmitiyas—to work on the sugar plantations of Trinidad, British Guiana, and other parts of the world add up to a long history of immense sadness and great courage. Ever since my teens, growing up in Bihar, when I first learnt of the fate of these country people of mine, I have repeatedly visited them in my dreams. Maybe I will never get to visit Fiji, Mauritius, Suriname, and other such places to which many a Bhojpuri-speaking man, woman, and child was forcibly transported to slave and enrich the British and, to a lesser degree, the Dutch or the French, but it does not matter. Seeing films and reading books about their past and their present fills me with sensations that I can hardly describe.
Programming the Caribbean

“Beyond the geographic and cultural identity that defines the Caribbean, is the more complex question of a Caribbean cinema aesthetic which has captured the imagination of some writers and critics. The search for the essence of Caribbean cinema has included theories of Creolite, diversity and Negritude from Martinique and Guadeloupe; Negrismo from Cuba; Indigenisme from Haiti; and Pan-Africanism from the English-speaking Caribbean and across the region as a whole. Such cultural movements have inspired some of the classics of Caribbean cinema that deal with the region’s experience of slavery or post-slavery communities.”

These words are from the pen of June Givanni, a Black film writer and programmer, who put together, for one edition of the International Film Festival of Kerala, a thought-provoking and seriously entertaining package of documentaries and fiction films from countries loosely clubbed together under the name of “Caribbean”. The films by Ové and Roopnaraine discussed here were part of the package assembled by London-based Givanni, who, as a child, migrated with her parents from Guyana.

The picture that often exists in people’s minds about the Caribbean being a haven of rum, calypso, carnival, and cricket to the exclusion of pressing realities like widespread poverty, violence, and spiritual devastation in the wake of fresh inroads by neo-colonialist forces is likely to be dispelled if they were to sit through films figuring here. It is about time that their narcotised gaze shifted from carnivalesque stereotypes to more credible and relevant identities relating to the Caribbean experience. To turn their faces away from historical and contemporary realities and, instead, allow themselves to be dominated by wish-fulfilling myths is an exercise in futility best avoided.
Vidyarthy Chatterjee writes about cinema, society, and politics. His most recent book is called About Nothing in Particular (Aksharik, Kolkata).
